# Coinage (stamped metal money) (`coinage`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by standard_weights_measures, copper_bronze
- Core idea: A coin is a piece of metal of fixed weight and fineness stamped by an authority that guarantees both, so it can be counted at a glance instead of weighed and assayed at every sale. The stamp transfers trust: people accept the coin because the issuer stands behind it and takes it back in taxes and fines. Minimum design that functions: one fixed weight per denomination, a fixed alloy checked by assay, dies that are hard to copy, a mint monopoly with harsh penalties for forgers and clippers, and plenty of small base-metal change for daily purchases. Round, full-struck flans and later milled (reeded) edges stop clipping.
- Pitfalls:
  - Debasing the coin to pay the ruler's debts: people notice within months, hoard the old good coins and prices rise (Gresham's law: when bad and good coin must be accepted at the same face value, the good coin disappears)
  - Fixing a gold-to-silver ratio by decree far from the market ratio: the undervalued metal is melted or exported
  - Believing coins invented money: Mesopotamia and Egypt ran on weighed silver, copper and barley and on written credit for some two thousand years before coins
  - Minting only valuable coins: a silver piece worth a day's wage is useless for buying bread, and the chronic shortage of small change hurt every pre-modern economy
  - Assuming coin value is just its metal: tax acceptance and the issuer's credit let good coins circulate above metal value, and that premium is exactly what tempts rulers to debase
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2500 BC onwards – silver weighed by the shekel (about 8.3 g) is the standard of value and of payment, often as cut rings and scraps (hacksilver); true coins only arrive with Achaemenid and Greek rule; egypt: New Kingdom – prices reckoned in weighed units (deben of about 91 g of copper, silver shat) without coins; coinage only under Persian and Ptolemaic rule (4th–3rd c. BC); greece: c. 630–600 BC – first coins of electrum (gold-silver alloy) in Lydia and the Ionian cities of western Anatolia (Ephesus Artemision deposit); c. 550 BC separate pure gold and silver coins, traditionally credited to Croesus though some scholars date them to the early Persian period; Aegina, Athens and Corinth strike silver from the 6th c. BC; china: by c. 6th–5th c. BC – cast bronze spade and knife money, an independent invention (exact start disputed); 221 BC Qin imposes the round coin with a square hole (banliang); 118 BC Han wuzhu coin, standard for some seven centuries; india: c. 6th–4th c. BC – punch-marked silver coins (karshapana), probably an independent development; dating disputed; rome: c. 211 BC – silver denarius; 3rd c. AD debasement of the silver coinage to a few per cent silver; 309 Constantine's gold solidus (1/72 Roman pound, about 4.5 g), stable for some seven centuries in Byzantium; africa: c. AD 270 – Aksum (Ethiopia) strikes gold, silver and bronze coins; islamic: 696–698 – Abd al-Malik's reform: purely inscribed gold dinar (about 4.25 g) and silver dirham replace Byzantine and Sasanian types; muhtasib inspectors check coin in markets; europe: c. 755–794 – Carolingian silver penny and the reckoning 1 pound = 20 shillings = 240 pence; 1252 Florence gold florin and Genoa genovino; 1284 Venetian ducat; 1550s screw-press minting in Paris; 1662 machine-milled coinage in England
- Read:
  - David M. Schaps, The Invention of Coinage and the Monetization of Ancient Greece (2004)
  - Thomas J. Sargent & François R. Velde, The Big Problem of Small Change (2002)
  - Glyn Davies, A History of Money from Ancient Times to the Present Day (1994)
